attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post. It is not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: Calling the expectation 'bonkers' is firm, unhedged language. It commits him to such chatbots not existing within a year, and the horizon and 'perfectly reliable' threshold are kept. The article title's 'probably' is not part of this sentence.

contract.note: The plain reading (general-purpose, perfectly reliable chatbots by 2025-02-23) is ordinary. Taking broad scope from the surrounding 'all queries' text is fair, and the contract does not stretch the claim for or against him.

evidence.note: OpenAI disclosure, October 2024, inside the window. It admits current models still hallucinate. It covers closed-book OpenAI models only.
OpenAI disclosure, February 2025, before the deadline. It says even the web-browsing deep research tool can hallucinate facts.
Claimed hallucination elimination on 37 RAGTruth samples with short factual passages. That falls far short of a general-purpose, perfectly reliable chatbot.

reviews.rationale: The deadline (2025-02-23) has passed. Dated disclosures up to February 2025 admit hallucinations continued even in retrieval-enabled systems. The only claimed hallucination-free result (Acurai) was a small, restricted test. No verified perfectly reliable general-purpose chatbot appears in the packet, so the support condition is met. Caveat: the outcome evidence is concentrated on OpenAI.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I do think ... will' is emphatic belief, not on the policy's list of hedges. It is a forecast with no deadline. The neurosymbolic remark is a possible route, not a condition, so leaving it out is correct.

contract.note: Reading 'reliably' as broadly trustworthy is fair given the context. The contract correctly says failures and elapsed time cannot contradict an 'eventually' claim.

evidence.note: International AI Safety Report, February 2026. Reliability is improving but failures persist. That neither shows eventual success nor rules it out.
HalluWorld preprint, May 2026. Progress is uneven and some hallucination types remain unsolved. This is not decisive either way.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. As of the evaluation date, the evidence shows partial improvement with continuing failures: no replicated demonstration of broad reliability, and no proof it is impossible. Neither the early-resolution support rule nor the contradiction rule is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Calling a six-month timeline 'naive' is firm and implies broadly reliable RAG will not arrive within six months. 'This' refers to reliably answering all queries via RAG, as the preceding text shows. Adding 'hallucination-free' slightly sharpens the wording but matches the context.

contract.note: Taking the deadline as six months from publication (2024-08-23) and the scope as broad query answering is the ordinary reading. Excluding restricted datasets follows his 'not just some obvious ones' framing.

evidence.note: CRAG v1 preprint, June 2024: top industry RAG systems answered only 63% of questions without hallucination, far from broad reliability.
Official KDD Cup results, 2024-07-30: winning scores of 28 to 48%. These are competition scores, not hallucination rates, but they show broad RAG answering was still incomplete.
Acurai company press release before the deadline, claiming 100% accuracy. Its validation was limited to RAGTruth, so it is a vendor claim, not independent broad evidence.
December 2024 paper, after the deadline but before the evaluation date. It shows the Acurai test used 37 samples with three factual passages each, which is restricted scope.

reviews.rationale: The deadline (2024-08-23) has passed. Independent benchmark and competition results from June and July 2024 show broad RAG question answering still made material errors. The one contrary claim, Acurai, came from a narrow, small-sample test. No verified broadly reliable RAG system appears, so the support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'We are kidding ourselves if we think' is firm and amounts to a negative near-term forecast. The following sentence, with 'very likely', is hedged but is not part of this claim. 'Near at hand' sets no explicit horizon.

contract.note: The one-year window is borrowed from nearby sentences, not supplied by this one. Even so, 'near at hand' ordinarily means imminent, and the surrounding six-month and one-year framing makes a 2025-02-23 endpoint a fair, ordinary reading. The contract itself flags that the result depends on this interpretation.

evidence.note: BBC independent test of four web-enabled assistants, run December 2024 and published 2025-02-11, before the deadline: 51% of answers had significant issues, including factual errors.
International AI Safety Report 2025, published within the window: hallucinations persist and mitigations are not fail-proof.
Legal RAG study, May 2024: RAG reduced hallucinations, but they remained substantial. It qualifies RAG's benefit and shows no solution.

reviews.rationale: On the contract's one-year reading, the deadline has passed. Independent evidence near the end of the window (BBC, February 2025) and the 2025 scientific assessment show deployed systems still made substantial factual errors, and no broadly validated solution emerged. The result does depend on the borrowed one-year horizon, which I judge a fair reading.
